Nadeshiko won the Women’s World Cup in 2011 and reached another final in 2015, while more established countries fell by the wayside. Japan have not replicated that success but did win the Women’s Asian Cup this year under the guidance of Nils Nielsen, who has since been succeeded by Michihisa Kano, and most of the biggest stars play outside the country, with 24 contracted to Women’s Super League clubs alone.

Japan are discreet about the secrets behind their success, particularly the easy-on-the-eye style that has become a trademark of the men’s and women’s teams, but one of those secrets lies in the Japanese Football Association (JFA) creating the JFA Academy.

There are three that take girls across the country of 123 million people: Fukushima, Sakai and Imabari. A fourth, Kumamoto Uki, is a boys’ academy only. Fukushima was the first to open, in 2006, with Sakai following in 2012 and Imabari in 2015.

Shota Mishio, an analyst for the national team when they conquered the world in 2011, recently coached in the Fukushima academy, which since the nuclear disaster that preceded their World Cup success by months has moved to Susono City. He offers an insight into how they are able not only to develop world-class individuals but to mould them into a successful unit for the national team.

The girls enter the academies at 13 and, other than in Fukushima, leave at 15. “The players are here until the age of 18,” Mishio says of Fukushima, which has five technical coaches dedicated to the girls. “We belong to the JFA, we are a coaching school with accommodation for players … the most important information I can give you is 25% of our original players have become senior national team players – that is a very high percentage.”

At the 2023 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand, five of Japan’s 23 players had come through the Fukushima academy. At the Paris Olympics a year later, it was seven, Mishio pointing to a “progression every tournament”.

One of them, Manaka Hayashi, is one of the more recent success stories. She graduated in 2022 and, after playing domestically for INAC Kobe, earned a move to the NWSL side Chicago Stars at the start of 2025. “We all had to apply for it, then the coaches come and watch us try out,” she says. “There could be 100 to 200 players who could apply, but only half a dozen get selected, so it’s not easy to get selected, it’s quite special.”

The way of playing is drilled into them from a young age, and is a big reason why Japan have enjoyed such success. “I’d say yes,” says Hayashi, adding: “The coaches emphasised a lot we had to be better technically. When you play against foreign teams, they are faster and stronger than us, so we had to be smarter to compete against them with quality on the ball. We had to be skilful on the ball to become better than other countries.”
